title: Multi-Agent Pipelines Over Encrypted Tunnels
description: Chain OpenClaw agents into production pipelines. Every hop encrypted, every agent authenticated, every message reliable.
seoTitle: Multi-Agent Pipelines Over Encrypted | Pilot Protocol Blog
author: Pilot Protocol editorial team

children.text: A single AI agent can answer questions. A pipeline of specialized agents can solve problems. The challenge is connecting them: finding the right agents, moving data between them, handling failures, and doing it all securely. This article shows how to build multi-agent pipelines using OpenClaw agents connected over Pilot Protocol encrypted tunnels -- from simple two-agent chains to complex DAG workflows with parallel branches and conditional routing.
Modern AI workflows chain multiple models and tools. A typical analysis pipeline might look like:
-- runs ML models or statistical analysis

Each agent is an OpenClaw instance running on potentially different hardware, in different locations, behind different NATs. The preprocessing agent might need fast SSDs. The analysis agent might need a GPU. The reporting agent might need access to a template rendering service.

The standard approach is HTTP APIs between each stage. This requires public endpoints (or VPN), TLS certificate management, retry logic, and circuit breakers at every hop. For 4 agents, that is 3 HTTP integrations to build and maintain.
With Pilot Protocol, the agents just trust each other and communicate. No HTTP servers. No TLS certificates. No VPN. The tunnel handles encryption, NAT traversal, and reliable delivery.
The simplest pipeline: one agent sends work to another and waits for results.

fields.code:
# Agent A: Send file and work description to Agent B (hostname: preprocessor)
pilotctl send-file preprocessor ./raw-data.csv
pilotctl send-message preprocessor --wait 10m --data \
  '{"description":"Clean and normalize the CSV: remove nulls, standardize dates, convert currencies to USD","params":{"input":"raw-data.csv","output_format":"parquet"}}'
# --wait prints Agent B's reply inline: the result JSON with the cleaned data location.
# Agent B answers with: pilotctl send-message <agent-a> --reply-to <message_id> --data '...'

# A reply that arrives after the wait is still saved to the inbox
pilotctl --json inbox --from preprocessor --latest

children.text: Agent A blocks waiting for the reply. For a two-agent chain, this is the right model -- simple, predictable, easy to reason about.
When independent tasks can run simultaneously, fan out to multiple agents in parallel:

fields.code:
# Orchestrator fans out to three specialists in parallel
# (In practice, the orchestrator spawns these as concurrent tool calls)

# Branch 1: Sentiment analysis
pilotctl send-message sentiment --wait 5m --data \
  '{"description":"Run sentiment analysis on customer reviews","params":{"model":"roberta-sentiment"}}' &

# Branch 2: Topic extraction
pilotctl send-message topics --wait 5m --data \
  '{"description":"Extract topics from customer reviews using LDA","params":{"num_topics":"10"}}' &

# Branch 3: Named entity recognition
pilotctl send-message ner --wait 5m --data \
  '{"description":"Extract named entities: products, companies, people"}' &

# Each command prints its branch's reply when it arrives; wait for all three
wait

children.text: The orchestrator sends all three tasks simultaneously. Each specialist works independently on its branch. When all three complete, the orchestrator merges the results. This is the MapReduce pattern applied to agent pipelines.

For fan-out to work well, the orchestrator needs to handle partial failures. If the sentiment agent fails but topic extraction and NER succeed, the orchestrator should still produce a partial result rather than failing entirely.

For pipelines where stages trigger asynchronously, use Pilot Protocol's pub/sub event stream. Every daemon runs an event stream on port 1002; the stages below all publish and subscribe on one node, named

fields.code:
# Stage 1: Data agent publishes when new data arrives
pilotctl publish coordinator pipeline.data.ready \
  --data '{"source": "api-feed", "rows": 15000, "path": "/data/batch-42.parquet"}'

# Stage 2: Preprocessing agent subscribes and auto-triggers
pilotctl subscribe coordinator pipeline.data.ready
# When event arrives, agent starts cleaning the data

# Stage 3: Analysis agent subscribes to preprocessed data
pilotctl subscribe coordinator pipeline.preprocessed.ready

# Each stage publishes completion events that trigger the next stage

children.text: The event-driven model decouples pipeline stages. No stage needs to know the address of the next stage -- it just publishes a completion event. Any agent subscribed to that topic picks up the work. This enables dynamic scaling: if the preprocessing stage is slow, spin up a second preprocessing agent subscribed to the same topic. Both agents receive every data-ready event, so give them a rule for which batches each one takes (for example, odd and even batch numbers).
Some pipelines need branching logic: if the data contains anomalies, route to the anomaly investigation agent. If the data is clean, route directly to analysis.

fields.code:
# Preprocessing agent evaluates the data and routes conditionally
pilotctl publish coordinator pipeline.preprocessed.anomaly \
  --data '{"anomaly_count": 47, "severity": "high"}'

# OR, if data is clean:
pilotctl publish coordinator pipeline.preprocessed.clean \
  --data '{"rows": 14953, "path": "/data/clean-42.parquet"}'

# Different agents subscribe to different topics:
# Anomaly investigator: pipeline.preprocessed.anomaly
# Standard analyzer: pipeline.preprocessed.clean

children.text: The routing logic lives in the publishing agent. It evaluates the data and publishes to the appropriate topic. Downstream agents do not need conditional logic -- they subscribe to their specific topic and process whatever arrives.

Hard-coded hostnames work for fixed pipelines. For dynamic pipelines, put the agents in a private network and pick the best available agent at runtime by hostname (name your GPU trainers with a recognizable prefix). Networks are created by the registry operator, so this assumes you run your own rendezvous and have added the agents to network 7:

fields.code:
# List members of the network, then pick a gpu-trainer by hostname
pilotctl --json network members 7
# data.nodes: [{"address":"7:0007.0C11.2A33","hostname":"gpu-trainer-1",...},
#              {"address":"7:0007.0C11.5D66","hostname":"gpu-trainer-2",...}]

# Send work to the first available agent and wait for its reply
pilotctl send-message gpu-trainer-1 --wait 30m --data \
  '{"description":"Train classifier on preprocessed data"}'

children.text: is offline, the send fails and the orchestrator falls back to
. Hostnames (and any tags the member list shows) tell the orchestrator what each agent does; a failed send tells it which agents are down.
With this pattern, a pipeline does not have to be configured in advance. The orchestrator picks peers at runtime, composes the workflow, and adapts when agents join or leave the network.
Distributed pipelines fail. Agents crash, networks partition, tasks time out. The pipeline must handle this gracefully:
If the worker does not respond within a deadline, the orchestrator retries with a different agent.
exits with an error (peer unreachable or no reply in time), pick another agent from the member list and retry.
For fan-out pipelines, collect whatever results arrive within the timeout. Report partial results with a note about which branches completed.
Design tasks so they can be safely retried. If the orchestrator is unsure whether a task completed, it can resubmit. The worker should handle duplicate submissions gracefully.

The event-driven model is naturally resilient. If a processing agent crashes mid-pipeline, the events it already published are consumed. The events it has not yet published simply do not trigger the next stage. The event stream does not store or replay events: a replacement agent that subscribes receives events published from then on, so a stage that must not lose work should record what it has processed, or have the upstream stage publish again.
Chain, fan-out, or event-drive. Pilot tunnels handle the networking.
